title: How to be a guest
hookLine: seven weeks visiting seven doors, one first idea at a time, in each tradition's own words

cards: Everyone pauses before eating, and you're not sure whether to bow your head. There's a word everyone knows but you. You take your shoes off only after noticing everyone else's by the door.
That's being a guest at a friend's family dinner, a different family from yours. Being a good guest is a skill, and most of us learned it by accident.
For the next seven weeks, the job is to be a guest on purpose, at seven doors. Today, silverware.

teach.b: Here's the plan. Seven weeks, seven visits: Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, the Catholic tradition, Islam and Sikhism. Each is a whole door on this app, with years of its own lessons.
One week in each, one first idea a day, the way someone at home in that tradition might first explain it to a friend. That's all it is: a visit. So, four house rules.
First, use their words. Hindus say dharma, Jews say Torah, Muslims say the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, Sikhs say Guru Nanak.
Learn the words the way the family says them, not translated into something more comfortable.

teach.h: NOT A CONVERSION, NOT A CONTEST.
teach.b: Second, a visit is not a conversion and not a comparison. Nobody is being recruited, and nobody is being ranked.
When an idea sounds like something from another door, let each keep its own meaning, the way Rumi and Marcus were kept apart. Third, where a family disagrees with itself, say so.
Every tradition has schools and arguments; name who says what rather than pick a side.
Fourth, don't pocket the silverware. It's easy to take a practice home, a candle, a chant, a bow, and strip away what it means.

Try things if you like, as a guest, and remember whose table you're at. There's an old line from the Taittiriya Upanishad, a Hindu scripture, often recited in India: let the guest be as God to you. That's a host's duty.
The guest's half of the bargain is to be worthy of it.

how: Visitors to temples, gurdwaras, mosques, synagogues and churches usually learn the house customs first: shoes, head coverings, dress, silence, and asking before taking photographs.

games.q: you're a guest at a friend's family dinner. everyone pauses before eating. you don't know the custom. what do you do?
o: pause with them, and ask later what it meant.
explain how your family does it.
games.why: a good guest follows the house rhythm and asks with curiosity afterward. that's the stance for all seven visits.

practice: Remember a time someone was a wonderful guest in your home, or a time you felt truly welcomed in someone else's. What did they do: listen more than talk, ask before touching things, say thank you in the right way?
Choose one simple thing you'll bring to these seven visits.
